question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the underlined word in the given sentence.
Try to be frugal with your hard-earned money.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Economical.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Frugal" means being careful and economical with money or resources; avoiding waste or unnecessary expenditure. (मितव्ययी / किफायती)
◦ Example: Despite earning well, she leads a frugal lifestyle and saves most of her income.

• "Economical" carries the same sense of being thrifty and prudent in spending, making it the closest synonym of "frugal" in this context.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Imprudent" (अविवेकी): Not showing care or thought for the consequences of an action; unwise — this is nearly opposite in meaning to "frugal".

• Option 3: "Negligent" (लापरवाह): Failing to take proper care over something; careless — unrelated to being thrifty with money.

• Option 4: "Honest" (ईमानदार): Free of deceit and truthful — a quality of character, not of spending habits.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "frugal": thrifty, prudent, sparing, austere, parsimonious.

• Do not confuse "frugal" (wisely economical) with "stingy"/"miserly" (unwilling to spend even when necessary) — frugal has a positive connotation while stingy has a negative one.

question:
Sentences of a paragraph are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the sentences in the correct order to form a meaningful and coherent paragraph.
A. It is considered the biggest carnival event in the world.
B. Rio carnival is celebrated every year before lent.
C. A typical Rio carnival is filled with floats, revelers and adornments from numerous Samba schools in Rio.
D. Every school is specially ordered to follow their parade entries.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. BACD.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Sentence B is the best opener as it introduces the subject of the paragraph — "Rio carnival is celebrated every year before lent" — establishing what the paragraph is about.

• Sentence A logically follows B, adding a key fact about the carnival introduced in B — "It is considered the biggest carnival event in the world."

• Sentence C then elaborates on what a typical Rio carnival looks like — "filled with floats, revelers and adornments from numerous Samba schools in Rio" — building on the idea of it being a grand event.

• Sentence D logically closes the paragraph, following up on the mention of "Samba schools" in C with a related detail — "Every school is specially ordered to follow their parade entries."

• Reading the sequence B-A-C-D together gives a smooth, logical flow of ideas from introduction to elaboration to conclusion.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 (ABDC) is incorrect because it starts with A ("It is considered the biggest...") without first telling the reader what "it" refers to — the paragraph needs B first to establish the subject.

• Option 3 (BCDA) is incorrect because it places C (details of a typical carnival) before A (the general claim about it being the biggest event), disturbing the general-to-specific flow.

• Option 4 (ACDB) is incorrect for the same reason as Option 2 — it opens with the pronoun-dependent sentence A before the subject "Rio carnival" has been introduced by B.

NOTE

• In paragraph/sentence-rearrangement questions, always look for the sentence that introduces the subject/topic (usually free of pronouns like "it", "this", "these") — that sentence must come first.

• Pronouns and linking words (it, this, such, therefore, however) are strong clues to which sentence must follow another.

question: Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Laproscopy.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Laparoscopy" — a surgical procedure in which a fibre-optic instrument is inserted through the abdominal wall to view the organs or perform minor surgery. The word given in Option 1, "Laproscopy", is misspelt.

• Spelling key: LA + PARO + SCOPY. Note the "a" after "p" (para-), which is often mistakenly dropped, giving the incorrect form "Laproscopy". The word is built from Greek lapara (flank) + skopein (to view).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Generate" — correctly spelt; means to produce or bring into existence.

• Option 3: "Intermittent" — correctly spelt; means occurring at irregular intervals, not continuous.

• Option 4: "Guise" — correctly spelt; means an external form or appearance, often a false or assumed one.

NOTE

• Other commonly confused medical/scientific spellings in SSC exams: arthroscopy, endoscopy, colonoscopy, diagnosis, haemorrhage.

• A quick trick for words with the "-scopy" suffix: they usually follow a Greek combining vowel pattern (e.g., micro-scopy, tele-scopy, lapar-o-scopy) — check the connecting vowel before "-scopy" carefully.

question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
A book market / was been operated by some readers / in the street when / they reached there.
option_3: was been operated by some readers
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. was been operated by some readers.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The segment "was been operated by some readers" contains a grammatical error — the double auxiliary "was been" is incorrect. Only one form of "to be" can be used before a past participle in the passive voice at a time.

• Rule — Passive voice auxiliaries: Use either a simple past passive (was/were + V3) or a past perfect/continuous passive (had been + V3 or was being + V3), but never combine "was" and "been" together as "was been".

• The correct form should be either "was operated by some readers" (simple past passive) or "had been operated by some readers" (past perfect passive, to show the action was completed before "they reached there").

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 ("they reached there.") is grammatically correct as it stands — a simple past tense clause.

• Option 2 ("A book market") is correct; it is simply the subject phrase of the sentence with no verb error.

• Option 4 ("in the street when") is correct; it is a prepositional phrase connecting the two clauses, with no grammatical fault.

NOTE

• Common double-auxiliary errors to watch for in SSC error-spotting questions: "was been", "is being being", "has been being", "will be being" — these combinations of two auxiliaries of "be" together (without a valid continuous-passive structure) are always wrong.

• The valid combination "was being + V3" (past continuous passive) exists and is different from the invalid "was been + V3".

question:
Select the most appropriate collocating word to fill in the blank.
The girl has ________ chances winning the match.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. high.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "High chances" is the standard, fixed collocation used in English to describe a strong likelihood or probability of something happening.

• Rule — Collocation: Certain words habitually pair together in English even though other words with similar meanings would be grammatically possible; "chances" collocates naturally with "high" or "good", not with words like "bountiful", "light" or "hefty", even though those words can mean "large" or "great" in other contexts.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 ("bountiful") is incorrect because although it means "abundant" or "plentiful", it does not naturally collocate with "chances" — it is typically used with words like "harvest" or "supply".

• Option 3 ("light") is incorrect because "light chances" is not a standard English expression; "light" collocates with words like "rain", "meal" or "sleep".

• Option 4 ("hefty") is incorrect because "hefty" collocates with words denoting size, weight or amount, such as "hefty fine" or "hefty price", not with "chances".

NOTE

• Other common collocations with "chances": slim chances, fair chances, remote chances, an outside chance.

• Collocation questions cannot always be solved by grammar rules alone — they must be learned as fixed word-pairings through reading and practice.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the underlined word.
No one was prepared for the environmental calamity that hit the town in the middle of the night.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Catastrophe.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Calamity" means a grave event bringing great loss, misfortune, or destruction; a disaster. (विपत्ति / आपदा)
◦ Example: The earthquake was a calamity that left thousands homeless.

• "Catastrophe" carries the same sense of a sudden, large-scale disaster, making it the closest synonym of "calamity" in this context.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Damage" (क्षति): Physical harm that reduces the value or usefulness of something — a possible consequence of a calamity, but not synonymous with the event itself.

• Option 3: "Degradation" (गिरावट): The process of being made worse in quality or condition, typically gradual — it lacks the suddenness and scale implied by "calamity".

• Option 4: "Stress" (तनाव): Mental or emotional strain — an unrelated, purely psychological meaning.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "calamity": disaster, cataclysm, tragedy, catastrophe, misfortune.

• Antonym of "calamity": blessing, boon, godsend.

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
Something which is worth believing
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Credible.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Credible" means able to be believed; convincing and worthy of belief or trust. (विश्वसनीय)
◦ Example: The witness gave a credible account of the accident.

• This one-word substitution directly matches the given phrase, "something which is worth believing".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Spurious" (नकली/जाली): Not genuine or authentic; false, though seeming to be real — nearly opposite in sense to "credible".

• Option 2: "Expedient" (सुविधाजनक): Convenient and practical, though possibly improper or immoral — relates to usefulness, not believability.

• Option 4: "Impending" (आसन्न): About to happen soon, usually something unpleasant — relates to time, not believability.

NOTE

• Other similar one-word substitutions: "Plausible" (seemingly believable/reasonable), "Authentic" (genuine), "Reliable" (able to be trusted).

• Do not confuse "credible" (believable) with "creditable" (deserving praise) or "credulous" (too ready to believe things, gullible) — these three words are commonly tested together in SSC vocabulary questions.

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.
somebody is following us.
option_3: We have been following by somebody.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. We're being followed by somebody.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "Somebody is following us" is in the Present Continuous Tense.

• Rule — Present Continuous Tense:
◦ Active: Subject + is/am/are + V-ing + Object
◦ Passive: Object + is/am/are + being + V3 + by + Subject

• Applying the rule: the object "us" becomes the subject "we"; the auxiliary "is" is replaced by "are being" (agreeing with "we"); the verb "following" becomes the past participle "followed"; and "somebody" becomes the agent with "by".
◦ Passive: We are being followed by somebody = We're being followed by somebody.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "had been following" is the active form of the Past Perfect Continuous Tense, not a passive form at all.

• Option 2 is incorrect because it merely repeats the original active sentence without converting it to the passive voice.

• Option 3 is incorrect because the passive auxiliary structure is wrong — it should be "being followed", not "have been following"; also "by somebody" cannot follow "following" in an active-form verb phrase like this.

NOTE

• The passive of the Present Continuous Tense always uses the structure "is/am/are + being + V3" — students often forget the word "being", producing the error seen in incorrect options.

• Compare: Present Simple passive = "is/am/are + V3" (no "being"); Present Continuous passive = "is/am/are + being + V3".

question:
The question below consists of a set of labeled sentences. Out of the four options given, select the most logical order of the sentences to form a coherent paragraph.
P. The division was usually based on temperature, which allows for different vegetation growth.
Q. Köppen's map used different colors and shades to represent the different climate zones of the world.
R. Wladimir Köppen developed a climate classification system at the end of the 19th century.
S. The system divides the world into five climate zones.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. RSPQ.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Sentence R is the natural opener as it introduces the subject of the whole paragraph — "Wladimir Köppen developed a climate classification system at the end of the 19th century."

• Sentence S logically follows R, explaining what that system does — "The system divides the world into five climate zones."

• Sentence P then follows up on "climate zones" from S, explaining the basis of that division — "The division was usually based on temperature, which allows for different vegetation growth."

• Sentence Q closes the paragraph with a further descriptive detail about how the zones were shown — "Köppen's map used different colors and shades to represent the different climate zones of the world."

• The chain R (who/what) → S (what the system does) → P (basis of division) → Q (how it was represented) gives a smooth, logical progression.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 (SPQR) is incorrect because it opens with "The system" (S), a phrase that presupposes the reader already knows which system is being discussed — this reference needs R to precede it.

• Option 3 (QPSR) is incorrect because it opens with Q, referring to "Köppen's map" before Köppen or his system has even been introduced by R.

• Option 4 (RPQS) is incorrect because it places P (basis of division into zones) before S (which first establishes that zones exist at all) — this reverses the logical cause-and-effect order.

NOTE

• When solving paragraph-jumble questions, identify the sentence that names the main subject/person without using a pronoun or defining article ("the system", "the map") — that sentence must be the opening sentence.

• Chronological/logical dependency (who developed it → what it does → how → detail) is a common structuring pattern in SSC paragraph questions.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
Fair-weather friends
option_1: A person who is friends with you during the night
option_2: A person who is friends with you every day
option_3: A person whose friendship cannot be relied on in times
option_4: A person who is friends with you in difficult times
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. A person whose friendship cannot be relied on in times.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Fair-weather friend" means a person who is friendly and supportive only when things are going well, but who cannot be relied upon or is absent during times of difficulty or trouble. (मतलबी दोस्त / स्वार्थी मित्र)
◦ Example: When I lost my job, I realised most of my colleagues were just fair-weather friends.

• The expression comes from sailing — fair weather is pleasant, calm weather; a "fair-weather friend" is one who stays around only in pleasant ("fair") circumstances and disappears when conditions turn stormy or difficult.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because the idiom has nothing to do with the time of day (night); it is about reliability during hardship, not the hour of friendship.

• Option 2 is incorrect because it describes the exact opposite of a fair-weather friend — one who is present every day, i.e., a true and dependable friend.

• Option 4 is incorrect because it also describes the opposite meaning — a fair-weather friend specifically does NOT stay by you in difficult times.

NOTE

• Related/contrasting idioms often asked in SSC: "A friend in need is a friend indeed" (a true friend helps in times of trouble), "Rain or shine" (in all circumstances, favourable or not).

• Other idioms formed with "fair": "By fair means or foul" (by any method, honest or dishonest), "Fair and square" (honest and just).

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.
The child broke many toys in the shop. He even threw the paintings.
option_1: Many toys in the shop have been broken by the child. Even the paintings were thrown by him.
option_2: Many toys in the shop were broken by the child. Even the paintings have been thrown by him.
option_3: Many toys in the shop were broken by the child. Even the paintings were thrown by him.
option_4: Many toys in the shop were broken by the child. He has even thrown the paintings.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Many toys in the shop were broken by the child. Even the paintings were thrown by him.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Both sentences, "The child broke many toys in the shop" and "He even threw the paintings", are in the Simple Past Tense.

• Rule — Simple Past Tense:
◦ Active: Subject + V2 + Object
◦ Passive: Object + was/were + V3 + by + Subject

• Applying the rule to sentence 1: "many toys" (plural) becomes the subject, so "were broken by the child" is used. Applying it to sentence 2: "the paintings" (plural) becomes the subject, so "were thrown by him" is used — both sentences must stay consistently in the simple past passive.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because the first clause wrongly uses "have been broken" (Present Perfect passive) instead of the required Simple Past passive "were broken".

• Option 2 is incorrect because the second clause wrongly uses "have been thrown" (Present Perfect passive) instead of the required Simple Past passive "were thrown".

• Option 4 is incorrect because the second clause "He has even thrown the paintings" has not been converted into the passive voice at all — it remains in the active voice.

NOTE

• When a passage contains more than one sentence, every sentence must be converted using the tense rule that applies to it individually — do not assume the whole passage shares one tense unless it actually does.

• Common trap: mixing Simple Past passive with Present Perfect passive forms across the two clauses of a compound conversion question.

question: Select the sentence that uses the idiom correctly.
option_1: Ranita was not selected for the job as she got cold feet.
option_2: Walking bare feet on grass gave him cold feet.
option_3: After too much cycling Arun got cold feet.
option_4: One can swim easily with cold feet.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Ranita was not selected for the job as she got cold feet.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "to get cold feet" means to become suddenly nervous or fearful before doing something, and to lose one's courage or resolve to go through with it. (हिम्मत हार जाना / घबरा जाना)
◦ Example: He got cold feet right before his wedding and almost called it off.

• In Option 1, Ranita losing her nerve/becoming anxious (and consequently not being selected) correctly fits this figurative sense of the idiom.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 is incorrect because it uses "cold feet" in its literal sense (feet that are physically cold from walking barefoot), not the idiomatic sense of nervousness.

• Option 3 is incorrect for the same reason — it refers to feet being literally cold after cycling, not to fear or hesitation.

• Option 4 is incorrect because it again uses "cold feet" literally, referring to the physical temperature of the feet while swimming.

NOTE

• Other idioms about fear/nervousness often tested in SSC: "To lose one's nerve", "To have butterflies in one's stomach", "To chicken out" (to withdraw out of fear).

• Contrast with idioms of courage: "To bite the bullet" (to face a difficult situation bravely), "To take the bull by the horns" (to confront a problem directly).

question:
Select the correct direct form of the given sentence.
The doctor said that they had performed their bit.
option_1: The doctor said, “We performed our bit.”
option_2: The doctor said, “We are performing our bit.”
option_3: The doctor said, “We have performed our bit.”
option_4: The doctor says, “We had performed our bit.”
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. The doctor said, “We have performed our bit.”

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given reported (indirect) sentence uses the Past Perfect Tense — "had performed".

• Rule — Narration (Indirect to Direct), Tense Backshift: When converting FROM indirect TO direct speech, a Past Perfect verb in the indirect sentence (had + V3) is converted back to a Present Perfect verb (have/has + V3) inside the direct quotation, since Past Perfect in indirect speech is the backshifted form of Present Perfect in direct speech.

• The reporting verb "said" stays as "said", and the direct quotation takes the corresponding present perfect form: "We have performed our bit."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "We performed our bit" (Simple Past) does not correctly backshift to "had performed" the way Present Perfect does; Simple Past in direct speech normally converts to Past Perfect only via a different route, and reversing it here does not match precisely.

• Option 2 is incorrect because "We are performing our bit" is Present Continuous, which would convert to Past Continuous ("were performing") in indirect speech, not Past Perfect ("had performed").

• Option 4 is incorrect because although the tense "had performed" matches, the reporting verb has wrongly been changed to "says" (present tense); since the indirect sentence uses "said" (past tense), the direct form must also use "said" to keep the narration consistent.

NOTE

• Full backshift chain for narration: Present Simple ↔ Past Simple; Present Continuous ↔ Past Continuous; Present Perfect ↔ Past Perfect.

• Always check BOTH the reporting verb tense and the reported verb tense when solving direct-indirect conversion questions — a common trap is changing one correctly but leaving the other wrong.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Demolish
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Ruin.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Demolish" means to pull down or destroy a building or structure completely; to ruin or wreck something entirely. (नष्ट करना / ध्वस्त करना)
◦ Example: The old cinema hall was demolished to make way for a shopping mall.

• "Ruin" carries the same sense of complete destruction, making it the closest synonym of "demolish" among the given options.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Create" (बनाना): To bring something into existence — the direct opposite of "demolish".

• Option 2: "Fabricate" (गढ़ना/मनगढ़ंत बनाना): To construct or manufacture something, or to invent a false story — relates to making, not destroying.

• Option 4: "Shape" (आकार देना): To give form or structure to something — again relates to construction, not destruction.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "demolish": destroy, raze, dismantle, wreck, tear down.

• Antonyms of "demolish": build, construct, erect, create.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Abundant
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Minimal.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Abundant" means existing or available in large quantities; plentiful. (प्रचुर / भरपूर)
◦ Example: The region has an abundant supply of natural resources.

• "Minimal" means of a minimum amount, extent, or degree; the smallest possible, which is the direct opposite of "abundant".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Aplenty" (प्रचुर मात्रा में): Means "in abundance" — this is a synonym of "abundant", not an antonym.

• Option 3: "Plentiful" (भरपूर): Also means existing in great quantity — again a synonym, not an antonym, of "abundant".

• Option 4: "Fertile" (उपजाऊ): Means capable of producing abundant growth or crops — related in sense to productivity/abundance, not its opposite.

NOTE

• Other antonyms of "abundant": scarce, sparse, meagre, insufficient, deficient.

• Be careful in antonym questions to avoid options that are actually near-synonyms of the given word (like Options 2 and 3 here) — they are common distractors.

question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
Children listens to people / speaking around them / for a long time before / they begin to speak.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Children listens to people.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The segment "Children listens to people" contains a Subject-Verb Agreement error.

• Rule — Subject-Verb Agreement: "Children" is the plural form of "child" and therefore always takes a plural verb. The verb should be the base form "listen", not the singular form "listens" (which is used only with third-person singular subjects like "he/she/it/a child").

• The corrected segment should read: "Children listen to people."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 ("speaking around them") is grammatically correct — a present participle phrase used correctly here.

• Option 3 ("they begin to speak") is correct; "they" (plural, referring to children) correctly takes the plural verb "begin".

• Option 4 ("for a long time before") is correct; it is simply a prepositional/adverbial phrase with no verb-agreement issue.

NOTE

• Other common irregular plurals that trip up subject-verb agreement in SSC questions: child/children, man/men, woman/women, mouse/mice, foot/feet, tooth/teeth — all take a plural verb.

• Remember: in the present simple tense, "-s/-es" is added to the verb ONLY for third-person SINGULAR subjects (he/she/it), never for plural subjects.

question:
Rearrange the parts of the sentence in correct order.
The issue of
P. compulsory vaccination is difficult
Q. multiple interests all protected by human
R. because the governments need to consider
S. rights law and strike a fair balance between them
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. PRQS.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Beginning with the fixed opening "The issue of", part P naturally completes it — "compulsory vaccination is difficult" — giving the core statement of the sentence.

• Part R logically follows, introducing the reason — "because the governments need to consider".

• Part Q then follows R, naming what needs to be considered — "multiple interests all protected by human".

• Part S completes the sentence, finishing the phrase begun in Q and adding the concluding idea — "rights law and strike a fair balance between them".

• Reading it together: "The issue of compulsory vaccination is difficult because the governments need to consider multiple interests all protected by human rights law and strike a fair balance between them." This is a complete, grammatically sound, and logically coherent sentence.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 (PQRS) is incorrect because it places Q ("multiple interests all protected by human") directly after P, breaking the sentence before the reason ("because...") has been introduced, and disrupts the logical cause structure.

• Option 3 (RSPQ) is incorrect because it starts with the reason clause "R" before the main clause "P" has even been stated, which does not fit after the given fixed opener "The issue of".

• Option 4 (QSPR) is incorrect because it produces a grammatically broken and meaningless sequence, starting with "multiple interests all protected by human" directly after "The issue of".

NOTE

• In parts-rearrangement questions, always check which part correctly and grammatically completes the fixed given opening phrase first — this usually narrows down the options quickly.

• Look for a reason/cause marker like "because" — it typically introduces the explanatory part of the sentence and must follow the main clause it explains.

question:
Select the correct spelling of the underlined word from the following options.
Handover that peace of paper to me so that I can evaluate the authenticity of his amorous claims.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. piece.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined word "peace" is a misused homophone in this sentence — the intended word, given the context "a piece of paper", is "piece" (meaning a portion or part of something), not "peace" (meaning a state of calm/absence of conflict).

• Since the sentence refers to a single sheet — **"that ___ of paper" — the singular form "piece" is required, not the plural "pieces"**.

• Spelling key: P-I-E-C-E — remember the mnemonic "a piece of pie" (both "piece" and "pie" begin the same way) to fix the "ie" order.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "peice" — incorrect; the letters "e" and "i" have been wrongly reversed (violates the "i before e" pattern used here).

• Option 2: "peices" — incorrect; carries the same "ie/ei" spelling error as Option 1, and is additionally the wrong (plural) number.

• Option 3: "pieces" — the spelling itself is correct, but it is the plural form, which does not agree with the singular determiners "that"/"a" used in the sentence ("that piece of paper").

NOTE

• Do not confuse "piece" (a part/portion) with the homophone "peace" (calm, absence of war) — one of the most frequently tested homophone pairs in SSC.

• Other tricky "ie/ei" spelling pairs: believe, receive, achieve, ceiling, ancient — remember the general rule "i before e except after c" (with exceptions like "weird", "seize").

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
The crowing witch released a _________cackle as she turned the boy into a beast.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. loud.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "cackle" refers to a harsh, shrill laugh or cry, and it is most naturally and commonly described as being "loud", especially in the dramatic context of a witch performing a spell/transformation.

• The context of the sentence — a witch turning a boy into a beast — calls for a strong, dramatic, and menacing sound, which fits with "loud" rather than a quiet or gentle one.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 ("gentle") is incorrect because a "gentle cackle" does not fit the harsh, dramatic tone associated with a witch's cackle while casting a spell.

• Option 2 ("low") is incorrect because a witch's cackle in such a dramatic, villainous context is conventionally loud and piercing, not quiet or subdued.

• Option 4 ("soft") is incorrect for the same reason as Options 1 and 2 — it contradicts the harsh, dramatic nature typically associated with a cackle in this context.

NOTE

• A "cackle" by definition already implies harshness; pairing it with "loud" reinforces the intended dramatic, sinister tone of the sentence.

• Fill-in-the-blank questions of this type test contextual/collocational appropriateness — always consider the tone and setting of the whole sentence, not just the dictionary meaning of each option.

question:
Rearrange the parts of the sentence in correct order.
We looked for
P. strong relationships at locations in the
Q. genome that are not well studied in
R. apple and looked for which compounds we
S. could identify and which had nutritional value
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. PQRS.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Beginning with the fixed opening "We looked for", part P naturally completes it — "strong relationships at locations in the".

• Part Q logically follows, continuing the phrase — "genome that are not well studied in".

• Part R follows next, naming the subject and continuing the sentence — "apple and looked for which compounds we".

• Part S completes the sentence — "could identify and which had nutritional value".

• Reading it together: "We looked for strong relationships at locations in the genome that are not well studied in apple and looked for which compounds we could identify and which had nutritional value." This forms a complete and logically coherent sentence.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 (QSRP) is incorrect because it places Q ("genome that are not well studied in") directly after the fixed opener, which is grammatically broken since "genome" cannot immediately follow "We looked for".

• Option 2 (QRPS) is incorrect for the same reason — it begins with Q right after the fixed opener, producing an ungrammatical, incomplete phrase.

• Option 3 (SPQR) is incorrect because it opens with S ("could identify and which had nutritional value"), which cannot grammatically follow "We looked for" at all.

NOTE

• As with all parts-rearrangement questions, first identify which part can grammatically and logically follow the fixed given opening phrase — this quickly eliminates most wrong options.

• Watch for repeated key nouns (here, "genome", "apple", "compounds") — they usually indicate the correct chain of ideas from general subject to specific detail.

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Swaminathan had a table on which all his things, his coat, cap, slate, ink-bottle, and books, were thrown in a confused (1)_______. He sat on his stool and shut his eyes to (2) _________ what work he had for the day: first of course there was Arithmetic – those five (3)_______ in Profit and Loss; then there was English – he had to copy down a page from his English lesson and write dictionary meanings of (4) _______ words; and then there was Geography. And only two hours before him to do all this heap of work and get (5) _______ for school.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. heap.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The passage describes Swaminathan's things — his coat, cap, slate, ink-bottle, and books — as being thrown together untidily on the table. The word "heap" (a disorderly pile of things) fits perfectly with the adjective "confused" used just before the blank, giving the natural phrase "a confused heap."

• Contextual clue: multiple different objects (coat, cap, slate, ink-bottle, books) being described together as a single messy pile is best captured by "heap", which specifically denotes an untidy, jumbled collection of things.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 ("deal") is incorrect because "a confused deal" is not idiomatic English; "deal" refers to an amount or a business arrangement, not a pile of physical objects.

• Option 3 ("order") is incorrect because it is contextually opposite to the intended meaning — "order" implies neatness and arrangement, while the passage describes disorganised, thrown-together items.

• Option 4 ("load") is incorrect because although "load" can refer to a quantity of things, it does not naturally combine with "confused" the way "heap" does; "a confused load" is not standard English usage.

NOTE

• Cloze-passage questions should always be solved by reading the sentence(s) around the blank carefully — the surrounding adjectives (here, "confused") and nouns often narrow down the correct collocation.

• Common collocations with "heap": a heap of trouble, a heap of rubbish, in a crumpled heap.

And only two hours before him to do all this heap of work and get (5) _______ for school.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. recollect.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence describes Swaminathan shutting his eyes to bring to mind the work he had for the day — this act of closing one's eyes to remember/call to mind something is best expressed by the word "recollect" (to remember or recall something from memory).

• Contextual clue: shutting one's eyes is a typical gesture people make while trying to mentally recall or go over a list of tasks already known to them, which matches "recollect" far better than the other options.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 ("guess") is incorrect because Swaminathan already knows what work he has for the day (Arithmetic, English, Geography, as described afterward) — he is not guessing at an unknown; he is recalling known facts.

• Option 3 ("imagine") is incorrect because "imagine" means to form a mental image of something not real or not yet experienced, whereas Swaminathan is thinking about actual, already-assigned schoolwork.

• Option 4 ("estimate") is incorrect because "estimate" means to roughly calculate or judge the value/amount of something, which does not fit the act of remembering one's homework.

NOTE

• Distinguish between similar "remembering" words: "recollect"/"recall" (to bring back to mind something previously known), "remind" (to cause someone else to remember), "reminisce" (to recall pleasant past experiences, usually nostalgically).

• In cloze passages, always check whether the missing word describes a real/known fact (favouring "recall/recollect") or an unknown/hypothetical one (favouring "guess/imagine").

solution_text:

• Contextual clue: the passage is describing homework tasks (Arithmetic, English, Geography) from a young schoolboy's point of view, and referring to sums/problems as "puzzles" reflects how such exercises would appear to him — as things to figure out.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 ("disputes") is incorrect because "disputes" means disagreements or arguments between people, which is unrelated to Arithmetic sums.

• Option 3 ("debates") is incorrect because "debates" refers to formal discussions or arguments on a topic, again unrelated to solving numerical problems.

• Option 4 ("conditions") is incorrect because "conditions" refers to circumstances or requirements/terms, not to arithmetic problems needing to be solved.

NOTE

• Words like "sums", "problems", and "puzzles" are near-synonyms in the context of school Arithmetic exercises.

• Contextual clue: the entire passage conveys a tone of the boy being burdened by a heavy amount of homework ("all this heap of work") — looking up "difficult" words fits this tone of a challenging workload far better than any of the other options.

• Option 4 ("visible") is incorrect because "visible" means able to be seen, which is meaningless in the context of needing to find out the meanings of certain words.

NOTE

• In this kind of contextual vocabulary-in-cloze question, look for the word that logically explains WHY an action (here, "looking up dictionary meanings") is needed — only unfamiliar/"difficult" words require a dictionary check.

• Related classroom vocabulary: "new words", "unfamiliar words", "difficult words" are commonly used interchangeably in describing vocabulary homework.

• Contextual clue: "get ready for school" is a common everyday collocation describing the process of preparing (getting dressed, gathering books, etc.) before leaving for school — none of the other options form this natural collocation.

Additional Information

• Option 2 ("fit") is incorrect because "get fit" refers to becoming physically healthy/in shape, which is unrelated to preparing to go to school.

• Option 4 ("fixed") is incorrect because "get fixed" would suggest being repaired or scheduled/arranged, which does not fit the context of personal preparation for school.

NOTE

• "Get ready" is a very common fixed phrasal expression in English meaning to prepare oneself for an activity or to leave for somewhere.

• Similar fixed expressions: "get dressed", "get set", "get going" — each pairs "get" with a specific adjective/participle to form an idiomatic meaning.
